clinician.final_diagnosis: Metastatic prostate adenocarcinoma with diffuse bone marrow replacement
clinician.trajectory_summary: An 86-year-old man presented with one month of progressive dyspnea on minimal effort, fatigue, and palpitations. Initial evaluation by a cardiologist identified arrhythmia and started metoprolol. A geriatrician's workup revealed hemoglobin 12.0 g/dL and markedly elevated PSA (130 ng/mL with free PSA >20 ng/mL), contrasting with a normal PSA two years prior. Prostate ultrasound showed normal size (10 cm³) without nodularity, but bone scintigraphy demonstrated probable metastases in the L4 vertebra and right iliac crest. The patient was referred to an oncologist who diagnosed metastatic prostate cancer and initiated degarelix (240 mg loading dose, then 80 mg weekly) as palliative treatment. Fifteen days after degarelix initiation, the patient presented to the emergency department with frank dyspnea and severe pancytopenia (hemoglobin 6.2 g/dL, platelets 51,000/µL, leukocytes 3950/µL), requiring blood transfusion. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy revealed markedly increased cellularity with non-hematological cell clumps and conglomerates, with diffuse bone marrow replacement by metastatic adenocarcinoma. PSA immunostaining was positive, confirming tumor cells of prostatic origin. After four cycles of chemotherapy, the patient showed no significant improvement and the oncology team transitioned to palliative care. The patient required hemotransfusion support twice during follow-up.
